newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: COSTELLO WELCOMES RETAIL TRADE AND BUILDING FIGURES
The Federal Treasurer Peter Costello has welcomed today's increase in retail trade and building figures.
Retail trade increased 2.9 per cent in May after declines over the previous two months, while building approvals are up 2.2 per cent.
Mr Costello has also welcomed the news from Moody's Rating Agency, that Australia's AA2 long term debt rating was improving.

He says a convergence of economic indicators, such as good retail trade, good building approvals and international recognition of the budget, make for a very positive outlook for the Australian economy.
NEW OPTUS CHIEF SAYS PAY-TV RESTRUCTURE NEEDED
The new head of Optus Communications says there is a strong need for a restructure of the pay television industry.
Peter Howell-Davies today addressed his first media conference since taking over as Chief Executive two weeks ago.

With a background of more than 30 years of international experience in telecommunications, Mr Howell-Davies says pay television in Australia does not provide what customers want in quality or quantity.
He says: "If I want to watch one sort of sport I have to watch Foxtel, If I want to watch a different type of sport I have to watch Optus Vision..."
Mr Howell-Davies says people do not particularly want to do that, and with mounting losses in the industry, he says Pay TV is not providing operators with an acceptable return.
Mr Howell-Davies says talks are underway with the other major players, Foxtel and Australis, on a major restructure.
Issues include infrastructure and program sharing, and the future of Rugby League.
And on the controversial issue of overhead cabling, Optus has indicated it intends to consolidate after rolling past 2 million homes.
ACTING PM SAYS HE DID NOT EXPECT FARMERS TO LIKE WIK LEGISLATION
The Acting Prime Minister, Tim Fischer, says he did not expect farmer organisations to give the Federal Government's Wik legislation a tick.
The National Farmers' Federation says it is disappointed with the draft legislation, and is continuing to call for blanket extinguishment of native title on pastoral leases.
Mr Fischer says some farmer organisations say the legislation goes further than the Prime Minister's 10-point plan.
He says the Government remains prepared to consult widely on the Bill, at the margin, but not on the core intent of Mr Howard's plan.

Mr Fischer admits a QC who recently went through the legislation, has said that in some areas, the legislation goes further than the 10 point plan, and the 8 additional undertakings in the Longreach letter.
WIFE OF MAN SHOT DEAD BY POLICE SAYS SHOOTING INDEFENSIBLE
The wife of Roni Levi, who was shot dead by Police at Sydney's Bondi Beach last Saturday, has called for the two officers involved to be suspended.
Melinda Dundas made the call during a media conference at Bondi this afternoon.
She also called for Police policy on 'when to shoot' to be changed.
Ms Dundas says Roni Levi's death was morally indefensible.
She says it should not have happened, describing the violence as excessive, appalling and unjustifiable.
Ms Dundas says her husband was not wearing his glasses at the time of the shooting and would have seen police as nothing but a blur.
COMPANY MAY TAKE RACIAL VILIFICATION CASE TO FEDERAL COURT
The company at the centre of a racial discrimination ruling says it will take its case to the Federal Court.
The Human Rights and Equal Opportunities Commission has awarded a Melbourne man $55,000 after being told he had developed severe depression and become suicidal after being racially abused.
Alex Rugema, a French citizen with Ugandan background, told the Commission the taunts occurred at the Southcorp Packaging Company.
But Southcorp General Manager, Barry Watts, says the company believes no racial discrimination took place.
Mr Watts says legislation states the ruling is not binding or conclusive, and if the company is disatisfied it may appeal to the Federal Court for a review.
AUSTRALIA INSTITUTE WANTS NEW INDEX OF NATIONAL WELL-BEING
The Australia Institute wants governments and commentators to use a new index of national well-being.
The Institute argues the Gross Domestic Product is a faulty measure.
Institute Director Clive Hamilton says the GDP rose during the AIDS outbreak because there was extra medical research and expenditure.
He says the new index, the genuine progress indicator, while not perfect, is much better because it takes in things such as the cost of crime, unemployment and environmental degradation.
Mr Hamilton says it suggests a drop in living standards in the past two decades, despite a rise in the GDP.
He says continued growth is relying more and more on the run-down on capital, including roads and machinery and the environment, which has serious implications for future generations.
GOUGH SAYS WIK LEGISLATION SHAMEFUL
Former Prime Minister, Gough Whitlam, says the Federal Government's draft Wik legislation is potentially the most disastrous and shameful of this century.

Speaking at the National Press Club in Canberra, Mr Whitlam said it was to the enduring credit of the former Keating Government that it refused to tamper with the Racial Discrimination Act when dealing with native title.
He says the so-called 10-point legislation serves no purpose other than the infinite delay and postponement of justice.
Mr Whitlam: "Unless there are negotiations now on the basis of acceptance of the law, we shall have subjected ourselves to endless litigation before our courts and shame before the world".
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
